role: Junior blender at a sauce-aroma baijiu distillery
headline: A brewing engineering graduate who spent a year turning sorghum on the distillery floor, now a junior blender in the blending room of a mid-sized sauce-aroma baijiu distillery on the Chishui River in Renhuai, Guizhou, telling apart the rounds of spirit in five tulip glasses every morning and making trial blends with a measuring cylinder every afternoon
unit: A mid-sized sauce-aroma baijiu distillery on the Chishui River in Maotai town, Renhuai, Guizhou (its own fermentation pits and a store of clay jars, with a blending room under the technical center)
level: You can roughly tell the first round of spirit from the seventh, and you can smell out the three classic types: sauce aroma, mellow-sweet, and pit-bottom. You can make a trial blend from the head blender's recipe, but you don't yet dare set the proportions yourself, and you've never had a hand in a full-scale blend
intro: The head blender pushes a tulip glass toward you and says that from today, your blind-tasting scores count in your appraisal. The blending room's windows face north, hand cream isn't allowed inside, and since the day you came in you've given up chili. As of today, before every batch this distillery ships, one glass of it has to pass your nose.
salary_note: Estimate: at a mid-sized sauce-aroma distillery in Renhuai, technical staff in the blending room get base pay plus a year-end bonus, a notch below the national figure for liquor blenders. In good years the bonus is generous; in years when the sauce-aroma market cools, it shrinks.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Running full-scale blends (around fifty tonnes) and translating them into process parameters on the production floor

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Market research and analysis of consumer taste to set the target style of a blend

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: At the mutton noodle shop below the dorm, the owner sees you coming and leaves out the chili, giving you a bowl of clear broth. The workshop men at your table have bowls that are all red; they laugh at you, and you laugh too.

Into the blending room, windows open twenty minutes to air it. A glance at the hygrometer: twenty degrees. You set five tulip glasses in a row on a white cloth, mouths down, and wait for the head blender to set the test.

Blind tasting. Five unlabeled glasses; you lift each one, smell it, take a small sip, roll it round your tongue, and spit into the spittoon. You write: third round, fourth round, fifth round, pit-bottom, one not sure. The head blender reveals the labels. You got one wrong.

To the store for samples. Rows of clay jars run further than you can see, each labeled with its number, its round and the year it was laid down. With a ladle you draw a little from the mouth of a jar into a sample bottle, label it, and write the jar number in your notebook.

The chromatography lab's report is in: total acids, total esters, the main esters and aldehydes. You enter them one by one into the base-spirit records and circle the jar that smelled a little scorched this morning.

Trial blends. Following the recipe on the head blender's sticky note, you measure each part with cylinder and pipette: so much third round, so much fifth round, a touch of old spirit to season. Shake, seal, date it, and put it in the cabinet to rest.

A walk through the distilling floor. It's the season of the Double Ninth sorghum loading, and the men are turning grain on the cooling floor, the red sorghum steaming, a sweet-sour smell. You crouch, grab a handful and hold it under your nose.

After work you walk a stretch along the Chishui River. Across the water are the lights of another distillery, and the whole street smells of spent grain. Back in the dorm you write today's wrong glass in your notebook: what it was like, and why you got it wrong.

ladder.title: Junior Blender
ladder.focus: Keep tasting records for the head blender, draw samples, build the base-spirit files, make trial blends to recipe. You make Grade 3 blender on accurate blind tasting, a good memory and a steady hand with the measuring cylinder.

ladder.title: Liquor Blender, Grade 3
ladder.focus: Choose base spirits, set proportions, make trial blends and test their stability on your own, and check the lab's chemistry against them. You move up on trial blends that pass the head blender's tasting and recipes you can reproduce reliably.

ladder.title: Senior Liquor Blender (Grade 2)
ladder.focus: Own the blend of one or more products, run full-scale blends of dozens of tonnes and release batches, and take part in tastings for new products. You move up on stable batches and new products that sell.

ladder.title: Head Liquor Blender (Head of the Blending Room)
ladder.focus: Run the blending room and the allocation of the base-spirit store, set the blend standards and sensory evaluation rules, train apprentices, and mediate with sales and production. You move up on consistent taste across the distillery's products and sensible use of stock.

ladder.title: Chief Liquor Blender
ladder.focus: Set the distillery's house style and its plan for laying down base spirits, sign off every batch that leaves, and represent the distillery at industry tastings. You hold the job on a taste that hasn't drifted in decades.

ai_tasks.name: Market research and analysis of consumer taste to set the target style of a blend
ai_tasks.how: AI can pull together sales data, e-commerce reviews and taste feedback on social media and boil them down into trends and style keywords. A person only spot-checks the conclusions and decides the final target against the brand's positioning.

ai_tasks.name: Screening and evaluating base spirits (bulk, supporting, carrying and seasoning spirits) and building a spirit database
ai_tasks.how: AI can help organize the base spirits' chemical data, build the database, search and compare. Whether a base spirit is good, or fit to season with, still has to be judged by a person tasting it and smelling it.

ai_tasks.name: Optimizing blend recipes with orthogonal experiments and sensory tasting, and producing and stability-testing trial blends
ai_tasks.how: AI can design the orthogonal experiments, analyze the data and predict how proportions relate to the measurements, cutting the number of trials. The trial blends are still made and tasted by a person, who also judges what the stability results mean.

ai_tasks.name: Running full-scale blends (around fifty tonnes) and translating them into process parameters on the production floor
ai_tasks.how: A full-scale blend means facing real spirit, real equipment and batch-to-batch differences on the spot, adjusting parameters there and then, and someone has to answer if it goes wrong. At most AI offers reference parameters and keeps the records.

ai_tasks.name: Setting and maintaining technical standards for blends (chemical specs, sensory evaluation rules, storage requirements)
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft the standard, tidy the format of the specs and check it's consistent throughout. The sensory rules and the limits on key specs have to be set by a person, who answers for the standard.

ai_tasks.name: Working with quality, production and sales on tastings, trial sales and feedback before a new product launches
ai_tasks.how: AI can compile the tasting notes, trial-sales feedback and lists of problems into a summary report. Talking across departments, running the tastings and deciding what to change still takes a person to coordinate and decide.

events.e_blind_right: A blind tasting of eight glasses, and you didn't get one wrong. When he'd revealed the labels the head blender didn't praise you; he just pushed across the tasting notebook he'd kept for twenty years and said you could start reading it.
events.e_cold: You came down with a heavy cold, and for a whole week your nose smelled nothing. The head blender told you to stay out of the blending room, and back in the dorm, frantic, you sniffed the vinegar bottle every day. The day you smelled sourness again, you nearly cried.
events.e_no_chili: Home in Zunyi for New Year, your mother fried a big plate of chili chicken, and you didn't touch it. She thought something had gone wrong for you out there, and came to your room that night to ask.
events.e_judge: You sat the provincial exam for baijiu judges. For the three days of the exam you ate only plain rice porridge, and in the blind tastings of dozens of glasses there was a trap glass hidden among the strong-aroma, light-aroma and sauce-aroma spirits. You passed, and the certificate is locked in a drawer in the blending room.
events.e_duanwu: At the Dragon Boat Festival, when the distillery makes its fermentation starter, you were sent to help in the starter room. The women treading the starter sang as they trod, and you trod all afternoon until your calves shook going downstairs; that night all you could smell on yourself was starter.
events.e_turbid: One winter a batch of finished spirit was bottled, and when the warehouse got cold a white haze formed in the bottles. A distributor phoned to ask if it had gone bad. You and the head blender investigated through the night; in the end the filtering step hadn't been held at the right temperature, and the whole batch was reworked.
events.e_boom: The sauce-aroma market is red hot, and bosses from out of province come to town by the carload to buy base spirit, the price different every month. The year-end bonus doubled, and you sent a sum home.
events.e_gc: The chromatography lab got a new instrument: one injection measures over a hundred flavor compounds, and its software can plot the base spirits as a map by flavor. You stared at the map all afternoon and found that two jars that smelled alike to you sat far apart on it.
events.e_love: Every time the new analyst in the chromatography lab handed you a report, there was a tiny clay jar drawn on the last page. One day you wrote on the back of a report, "this jar smells of caramel," and handed it back.
events.e_dealer_dinner: At the distributors' conference the boss had you go up and talk about the blends. Afterwards you were dragged to dinner, and a whole table took turns toasting you. When you taste you always spit; that night you couldn't, and the next morning your nose was numb until noon.
events.e_wedding: You got married. The spirit at the banquet was a small batch you'd blended yourself, with no label. Your father-in-law took a sip and asked how much a bottle like this costs.
events.e_ai_recipe: The technical center is trialing recipe software: feed it the base spirits' chromatography data and it offers several sets of proportions to choose from. Its first suggestion made you frown at the first sniff; the third only needed a touch more seasoning, and you built on it, changing two milliliters.
events.e_downturn: The sauce-aroma market cooled, several small distilleries in town stopped production, and your distillery's stock filled three warehouses. The year-end bonus was cut in half, and at the staff meeting the boss said the ones who make it through will be the ones whose spirit is good.
events.e_master_retire: The head blender who trained you retired. On his last day he sat in the blending room all afternoon, smelling one by one the dozens of jars of seasoning spirit he'd laid down, and when he left he handed you the key to the cabinet.
events.e_child: Your child was born. You waited outside the delivery room all night, and at dawn, catching the smell of disinfectant in the hospital corridor, you couldn't help scoring it in your head.
events.e_big_batch: For the first time you ran a fifty-tonne blend. Dozens of jars of base spirit were pumped into the big tank to the recipe and circulated overnight; the next day you drew a sample and smelled it, a hair off the trial blend, and only after adding three more jars of old spirit did you feel easy enough to sign.
events.e_house: You put down a deposit on a flat in Zunyi city, where your child will go to school. Every weekend you drive over an hour back, and first thing Monday you're back by the Chishui River.
events.e_acquired: A big group from out of province bought the distillery, and the first thing the new general manager did was have you write up every product's recipe as a standard document. You wrote for three months, and at the end of every document you added one line: tasting takes precedence.
events.e_award: A spirit you designed won gold at an industry tasting, and the medal hangs in the middle of the distillery's showroom. The boss came to the blending room to shake your hand, and you were still holding an unwashed tulip glass.
events.e_apprentice: The new junior blender kept mixing up the fourth round and the fifth. You didn't scold him; every morning you set him three glasses of just those two, for a month, and he stopped getting them wrong.
events.e_uric: Your health check had a red arrow beside uric acid. The doctor asked if you drink; you said every day, and then that you spit it all out. The doctor didn't believe you, and told you to go to fewer dinners.
events.e_old_bottle: An old customer brought in a bottle from over ten years ago, from your distillery, wanting to know if it was still drinkable. You poured a little into a glass and smelled the jar of seasoning spirit the head blender used that year. You remember its number.
events.e_palate_age: You notice you're less sensitive to sourness now; in one blind tasting a high-acid glass nearly slipped past you. You've started having your apprentice taste first, then going through his notes against yours.

c_designer.title: Go for Liquor Blender, Grade 3
c_designer.situation: The distillery assesses once a year, and Grade 3 means handing in three trial blends with proportions you set yourself, blind-tasted by the head blender and the technical center together. Two of yours have had his nod; the third you're still reworking.

options.label: Apply this time
options.result: You reworked the third blend to its seventh version, and the day you handed it in your palms were soaked. In the blind tasting the head blender ranked your glass second.

options.label: Wait until next year
options.result: You said the third wasn't good enough yet. That year you made five more trial blends, and when you applied the next year, every one you handed in was your own choice.

c_big_brand.title: The big distillery in town comes poaching
c_big_brand.situation: A big listed distillery in town is hiring blenders, offering thirty percent more than you earn, with social insurance paid on your full wage. You'd be one of dozens in a big blending room, and your name would never be on any product.

options.label: Go to the big distillery
options.result: Their base-spirit store is so big you need an electric cart, and there's more seasoning spirit than you could smell in a lifetime. You're in a team of a dozen, handling one step of one product every day.

options.label: Stay at this distillery
options.result: You turned it down. That afternoon you stayed a while longer in the store, smelling jar by jar the old spirit the head blender had laid down.

c_ai_blend.title: Lead the recipe system or not
c_ai_blend.situation: The technical center is teaming up with a software company to turn years of chromatography data and tasting records into a recipe recommendation system, and wants you to lead it. The old masters say that once what's in your nose becomes numbers, it isn't that taste anymore.

options.label: Lead it
options.result: You spent a year matching thousands of tasting records to chromatography data one by one, and every one had to spell out which kind of scorched "scorched" meant and which kind of sweet "sweet" meant. Once the system went live, trial-and-error on blends fell by half.

options.label: Turn it down
options.result: The technical center found someone else. You glance at the system's proportions now and then, and most of the time still go by your own nose.

c_cheap.title: Make a cheap spirit or not
c_cheap.situation: The market is bad and the stock is piling up, and the boss wants a cheap plain-bottle spirit to move volume, blended from young base spirit and crushed-grain spirit into something that "drinks like the real thing." You know a spirit like that will sell, and you know it will damage the name.

options.label: Take it on, do it as well as you can
options.result: You picked through the cheap base spirits again and again, and in the end held it up with a little good seasoning spirit. It sold very well, and in a drinkers' group chat someone said, "at this price, that's honest."

options.label: Argue with the boss
options.result: You said better to sell less than give people a headache. The boss's face darkened, and in the end the spirit was blended by someone outside. Your bonus that year was noticeably smaller.

c_senior.title: Go for Senior Liquor Blender
c_senior.situation: Senior grade means presenting a product you're responsible for: from trial blend to full-scale blend, the tasting and chemistry of three shipped batches all have to be stable. One of your products is on its third batch, and one figure on the chromatograph keeps drifting.

options.label: Apply this time
options.result: You spent a month in the store, swapped two jars of base spirit, and the third batch finally held. At the panel a judge asked why you swapped those two jars, and you said they smelled like they were fighting.

options.label: Steady it one more year
options.result: You said you'd wait until the fourth batch was stable too. That year you made trial blends for two new products.

c_oem.title: Go out and do custom spirits yourself
c_oem.situation: A friend in town is in the custom spirits business: buying base spirit from distilleries, blending it, and selling it under other people's labels. He wants you in: you handle the blends, he handles sales, and he says one year of it would equal three of yours at the distillery.

options.label: Go in with him
options.result: You rented a little courtyard in town as a blending room, and handled everything yourself, from choosing base spirit to bottling. In the first year you took custom orders from dozens of work units, and tasted every spirit before it shipped.
options.end: You opened your own blending workshop in Maotai town, making custom spirits for work units and restaurants around the country; before every batch ships, you smell it once in the courtyard.

options.label: Stay at the distillery
options.result: You said you still wanted to take one taste all the way at one distillery. Your friend's business has had its ups and downs, and a few times he's asked you to come and smell a batch.

c_room.title: Take over the blending room
c_room.situation: The head of the blending room is moving to the technical center, and the boss wants you to take over: a dozen people, the allocation of all the distillery's base spirit and the blend standards, arguments with sales and arguments with production. The other candidate was poached from a big distillery outside and has more years than you.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Every day you check the store's inventory sheet first, then go into the blending room to taste. Sales want new products and production wants to save material, and you talk each of them round in the middle; back at the dorm at night you're still leafing through the tasting notebook.

options.label: Let him have it
options.result: The man from outside took over, and you still look after your few products. When he's unsure about a trial blend, he carries the glass over to your desk.

c_teach.title: Teach blending at the college
c_teach.situation: The brewing college in Renhuai has asked you to teach tasting and blending. Winter and summer holidays, no more business dinners, a bit less pay than the distillery. The college says its students are missing someone who's come out of a blending room.

options.label: Go and teach
options.result: In the lab you set five glasses in front of the students and, the way your old head blender did, have them write down what each glass is like, and why.
options.end: You became a tasting teacher at a brewing college in Renhuai, turning out a class of junior blenders every year; in the blending rooms of several distilleries in town, someone is using the tasting vocabulary you taught.

options.label: Stay at the distillery
options.result: You said a few more years. You promised to give two lectures a term at the college, and after each one you go back to the distillery and carry on tasting.

c_chief.title: Chief Liquor Blender or not
c_chief.situation: The boss says the distillery will name a chief: every batch that ships will carry your final signature, and you'll plan decades of base-spirit reserves. Once you sign, whenever a batch goes wrong, your name is the one on it.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Every week you walk through every store, deciding which jars get used this year and which are kept for twenty years from now. Before you sign for any batch you smell it yourself, and you sign very slowly.

options.label: Put your apprentice forward
options.result: You pushed your apprentice up and still taste every morning. Before he signs, he often pushes the glass across to you.

endings.retire: On your last day you still went into the blending room at half past eight, opened the windows twenty minutes to air it, and set five tulip glasses in a row on the white cloth. Your apprentice set you one last blind tasting, and you didn't get one wrong. Before you left you put the tasting notebook and the key to the seasoning-spirit cabinet on his desk, without a word of instruction.
endings.burnout: Those years brought too many dinners and more and more red arrows on your health checks, and one morning you lifted a glass and found you couldn't smell anything at all. You only heard half of what the doctor said. You handed in your resignation and went back to Zunyi. Later, old colleagues from town would bring trial blends for you to smell, and you'd say a word or two.

stages: Your mornings are in the blending room: the head blender sets a blind tasting, you write notes and scores, and the glass you get wrong goes into your notebook. Afternoons you draw samples from the clay jars with a ladle, send them to the chromatography lab, and enter the total acids and esters alongside what you smelled, the scorched, the sweet, the pit-bottom, into the base-spirit files; then you make trial blends to the head blender's sticky notes with a measuring cylinder. Not one proportion is yet your own.

You set the proportions yourself now: pick a dozen jars from the files, third round for the base, fifth round to lift the aroma, a little pit-bottom to hold it, then seasoning spirit to find that last touch. When a trial blend is done you taste it first, then carry it to the head blender; if he shakes his head you go back and rework it, and a recipe reaching its fifteenth version is normal. When the lab report and your nose disagree, you believe both, and go and smell it again.

A product is yours now: from trial blend to a full-scale blend of dozens of tonnes, from the tank circulating to the last sample before bottling, and whether each batch is released needs your signature. When sales hold a launch tasting, you stand on stage explaining why the spirit is blended the way it is; when distributors say it gives a headache or isn't fragrant enough, the calls come to you as well. You've started training a young newcomer to the blending room.

The blending room's dozen people are yours, and so is the allocation of the distillery's base spirit: which jars get used this year and which are kept, how much new product sales want and how much finished spirit production needs, you lay out square by square on the stock sheet. You set the blend standards and the sensory evaluation rules and run a blind tasting for the whole room every week; in meetings with the boss, what you say most is: that jar can't be touched yet.

You set this distillery's taste. Every batch that ships carries your final signature, and the plan for decades of base-spirit reserves is in your cabinet; you represent the distillery at industry tastings and come back to tell the technical center about other distilleries' spirits. You rarely make trial blends anymore; in the mornings you still taste a set, and in the afternoons you walk the stores, looking jar by jar at spirit that won't be opened until after you've retired.
work: The head blender has you sample all two hundred jars of fifth-round spirit in the east store. You ladle jar by jar and label bottle by bottle, and on the third day find a jar whose number doesn't match the files; it takes an afternoon to trace, and someone miscopied one digit when it was laid down.

Making a trial blend to the head blender's note, the seasoning spirit has to go in at three parts per thousand. You draw it into the pipette three times before you dare let it in; you shake it and smell it, and the head blender says from behind you: one drop more and it's ruined.

The chromatography lab says one jar's ethyl acetate is high. You go to the store and smell it, and there is a sour sting to it. You mark it "under observation" in the files, and when you smell it again three months later the sting has settled.

The first recipe you set yourself took fourteen versions. You carry the fourteenth to the head blender, who smells it a long time and says leave the empty glass until tomorrow morning. The next day the bottom of the glass is still fragrant, and he nods.

An old distributor says this year's spirit is "thinner" than last year's. You set the trial blends from both years side by side and taste them, find this year used a little more third round, and swap in two jars of older base spirit.

On the lab report two jars' data are almost identical, but to you one smells round and one astringent. You add each to the same trial blend separately, and the astringent one tightens the whole glass. In the files you write: the data can't see it.

The fifty-tonne tank has circulated all night, and you go to draw a sample at four in the morning. It's cold on the platform at the top of the tank; you take a smell, close to the trial blend, then wait until seven to draw a second before you sign the release form.

At a launch tasting, a distributor says the new spirit is "not sauce-y enough." You don't argue; after the meeting you invite him to the blending room, set out three glasses and let him say which is sauce-y enough. He points to one. It's the youngest.

The young blender you're training does his first calculation for a full-scale blend and misreads a jar's alcohol strength by one decimal place. You don't say anything in front of the others; you sit with him and his spreadsheet and work it through again.

Sales want thirty percent more new product next year. You pull the store's inventory sheet and work at it all evening: there's only enough good base spirit for twenty. In the meeting you put the sheet on the screen and say the other ten waits two years.

Running a blind tasting for the whole room, ten people on the same set, one glass's scores are wildly spread. You don't say who's right; you have each person say what they smelled, and only then do you reveal the label.
Revising the sensory evaluation rules, you split "scorched aroma" into three: caramel, roasted grain, burnt pan. Newcomers scoring to the rules come out far more consistent than before.

Before a batch is released, you smell a trace of rancid oil in the very last sample that shouldn't be there. You don't sign; you have the bottling line stopped and checked, and it turns out a newly replaced length of pipe wasn't flushed clean.
In the store you choose this year's jars to seal away, picking thirty of the best fifth-round, and chalk on each one the year to open it, by which time you'll have been retired several years.

At an industry tasting out of province, dozens of judges taste the same set. Back home you tell the technical center about other distilleries' spirits, and coming to a rival's new product, you say: their seasoning spirit is older than ours.
past: You grew up in a township in Zunyi. Your grandfather distilled at a little village distillery when he was young, and every New Year he poured a tiny cup for you to smell, saying good spirit lets you smell the grain.

In your last year of high school you saw the words "Brewing Engineering" on the application form, remembered your grandfather's cup, and put it first. Your father said studying that gets you into a distillery, and you'll never go hungry.

At university you studied microbiology and fermentation engineering. The first time you analyzed spirit on a gas chromatograph in the lab, you stared at the peaks on the screen and couldn't understand how they could be that aroma.

In third year you did a placement at a Renhuai distillery, loading the still, cutting the spirit and spreading the grain to cool alongside the workshop men. One of them caught a little of the spirit as it ran, rubbed it between his palms and smelled it, and knew whether that still was good.

After graduating you joined this distillery and were first assigned to the distilling floor. At the Double Ninth loading you turned grain on the cooling floor with the men for a year, and the calluses on your hands haven't gone yet.

The head of the blending room came to the floor to pick people and set five glasses in front of a few of you young ones. You got three right, and for the two you got wrong you explained why you'd got them wrong, and he took you with him.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Guizhou's urban employee pension scheme. The distillery paid in on your actual wage with few gaps, and with the company annuity you get about half your last monthly salary in retirement; being rehired as a tasting consultant brings in a separate income.
scenes: Your first week of retirement you still wake at half past eight, get up, push open the window and take a deep breath, smelling for spent grain on today's wind.

The distillery asks you to be a tasting consultant, back twice a month. You don't make trial blends anymore; at blind tastings you just sit in the back row and listen to the young ones say what each glass is like.
Of the thirty jars you sealed away years ago, one has reached its year. Your apprentice asks you back to draw the first ladle; you take a smell and say it can rest another five years.
For the first few months back in Zunyi you didn't touch any spirit, and even walked round the smell of it in restaurants.
Little by little your nose came back. One day your mother fried chili chicken and you could tell she'd switched to another stall's chilies this year. She said that nose of yours wasn't wasted.
An old colleague from town came to see you with a trial blend. You took one smell and said a little too much third round. He laughed and said that's exactly what you used to say to him.
For the first month after leaving the blending room, every morning you wanted to find five glasses to set in a row; finding none, you set out five teacups.
The young man you trained has become head of the blending room, and he sends a photo: the first page of his tasting notebook, with a line you once wrote for him copied out on it.

On the supermarket shelf there's a row of sauce-aroma spirits, and you read the back labels one by one. Finding one from your old distillery, you buy a bottle, take it home, have a sip, and say it's still that taste.

Lots of distilleries use chromatography data and recipe systems now, and trial-and-error on blends has dropped by more than half. But before every batch ships, that last glass still needs someone to lift it and smell it.

You still don't eat much chili. Home for New Year, the family cooks a dish without chili just for you. You drink a small cup of spirit, roll it round your mouth, and swallow; this time you don't have to spit.
You take your grandson walking by the Chishui River. The water is still red, and there are more distilleries on the banks. Your grandson says it stinks here. That's the smell of grain, you say.

closing.retire: One morning many years later, you are making tea on the balcony, and you hold the cup under your nose for a long time, then give it a score in your head and tell no one.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you sit in the courtyard of your home in Zunyi while next door the neighbors steam their homemade rice wine. When the wind brings it over you close your eyes and say: they steamed the rice well this year.
closing.end: Many years later, sorting through old things, you find a tulip glass with a faint fragrance still at the bottom. You wash it clean and set it on the windowsill, facing north.
